summary: Discusses operational aspects of keys and signatures used with the KEY and SIG DNS resource records, such as managing and protecting them in practice. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 4641.

plainLanguage.summary: Keeping signatures for the internet's phone book needs good habits, such as who looks after the keys and when to change them. This document gives that advice.

subtitle: How to generate, protect, and rotate the cryptographic keys that secure DNS.

tldr.problem: DNS uses cryptographic keys to verify that domain name information is authentic. These keys must be generated carefully, rotated regularly, kept secure, and sized appropriately to resist attack.
tldr.mechanism: This document provides operational guidelines for generating strong keys, choosing appropriate key lifetimes from 13 months for long-term offline keys to days for online transaction keys, selecting RSA and DSS key sizes that balance security and performance, and storing private keys offline away from the network wherever possible.
tldr.outcome: Operators who follow these practices reduce the risk that their DNS zones could be forged, and protect the most critical keys—especially the root zone key—with the strongest safeguards.

facts.label: RSA key size for high-level zones

today: RFC 2541 is an Informational RFC published in 1999 and is the original guidance on DNSSEC operational practices. It has been obsoleted by RFC 4641, which updated this guidance.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Domain Name System Security Extensions use cryptography to verify that domain names and addresses have not been forged. The strength of these protections depends on careful operational practices: how keys are generated, how long they are used, how large they are, and where they are stored.

This RFC describes the operational considerations for managing the KEY and SIG resource records that hold these keys and signatures in DNS. It pays special attention to high-level zones, which control many subdomains, and the root zone, which controls the entire DNS namespace.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS uses keys to prove names and numbers are real. This guide explains how to make good keys, keep them safe, and change them when needed.

sections.title: Key Generation and Lifetimes
sections.content:
Careful key generation is essential. The strongest algorithms are useless if an adversary can guess or reduce the search space of the key. All keys should be generated offline, away from the network, using equipment isolated by an air gap or secure hardware.

No key should be used forever. The longer a key stays in use, the greater the risk it will be compromised through accident, espionage, or mathematical attack. Long-term keys kept offline should have a lifetime around 13 months with annual replacement. Keys used for online transaction security should be replaced every 36 days or more often. However, keys that are too short-lived (less than 3 minutes) cause excessive overhead from constant re-signing and cache staleness. The RFC recommends balancing these concerns based on the zone administrator's local conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: Keys are like combination locks. Make them in secret, not connected to anything. Don't use the same lock forever—change it yearly if it's really important, monthly if you use it a lot. But not so often you're always changing it.

sections.title: Key Size and Cryptographic Algorithms
sections.content:
Larger cryptographic keys are more secure but slower to use. They also make DNS records bigger, which increases the risk that responses will overflow UDP packets and require slower TCP connections.

For RSA keys, the recommended minimum is 704 bits for data security, though high-level zones may want 1000 bits or more. The relationship is asymmetric: increasing from a 640-bit to a 1280-bit modulus only doubles verification time (roughly with the square of length) but may increase the effort to break the key by over 2^900 (to the 1.6 power of the modulus).

DSS keys of the same length are roughly as strong as RSA keys, but produce significantly smaller signatures, which can be an advantage in DNS.
sections.plainLanguage: Bigger locks are harder to pick, but they take longer to use. The choice is yours, but 700 bits is pretty good for a lock on data.

sections.title: Protecting Private Keys
sections.content:
Zone private keys should be kept in offline, non-network-connected, physically secure machines only. The zone file master copy should live there too. Periodically, an offline application can be run to add signatures and authentication records, then the augmented file can be transferred by sneaker-net to the primary server on the network.

This one-way information flow prevents an attacker who compromises the networked server from tamper with the master zone file. Dynamic updates that require frequent signing are an exception: at least a private key for updating the SOA and NXT chain must be online, but even then the master copy should remain offline. Secure resolvers must be configured with trusted public key information that is also protected from tampering.
sections.plainLanguage: The real master copy stays in a locked room not connected to anything. When you need new signatures, you plug in a drive from that locked room, sign the data, and bring the drive back. That way, hackers can't get to the master.

sections.title: High-Level and Root Zone Keys
sections.content:
Higher-level zones are more sensitive than lower ones: anyone who breaks the security of a zone controls all of its subdomains (except where resolvers have locally configured a subdomain's key). The root zone is the most critical: control of the root would grant an attacker authority over the entire DNS namespace.

The root zone private key must always be kept offline. However, frequently rotating it would require updating all resolvers worldwide, which is extremely difficult. To solve this, there will be a meta-root key used very rarely to sign a sequence of regular root keys with overlapping lifetimes that can be rolled out gradually. The meta-root key itself may be kept for an extended period, such as 10 to 15 years, and must be stored with the utmost care.
sections.plainLanguage: The root key is the most important lock in the internet. It has to be in a super-safe place. Because you can't easily change it everywhere, you use a backup key to sign replacement keys so you can swap them out slowly.
